title: The Company That Bought Itself With Paper

beats.text: In seventeen nineteen, Paris got rich on a colony nobody had seen.
Imagine you're on the rue Quincampoix, a narrow street jammed with buyers.
John Law's Mississippi Company sells shares at five hundred livres.
Rumor says Louisiana is full of gold.
Within a year, the same share costs ten thousand.
Even maids get rich. Paris calls them millionaires.
So where's all that money coming from?
You see, picture a board game where the banker prints cash whenever you run short.
That's Law. He also runs the royal bank, whose notes buy the shares.
In March seventeen twenty, he fixes the price at nine thousand and buys back shares with fresh notes.
So everyone sells, and the paper multiplies.
By December, the share is down to one thousand, and the notes have lost half their value.
Law flees France. Nobody had been paying for the company. It was paying for itself, in paper.

facts.claim: Mississippi Company shares started at about 500 livres (January 1719)
Shares peaked near 10,000 livres in December 1719 / January 1720, within about a year
Trading took place on the rue Quincampoix in Paris, crowded with buyers
John Law was a Scot (born Edinburgh 1671) who ran the company and the bank (Banque Générale, later Banque Royale) that issued paper notes
Rumours of gold and silver in Louisiana drew investors
Working-class people (maids, servants) invested and got rich; the word millionaire came into use for the beneficiaries
The bank issued more notes to fund share purchases; notes in circulation multiplied (about 1 billion livres by January 1720, 2.2 billion by May 1720)
In March 1720 the price was fixed at 9,000 livres, with shares bought back for notes
By December 1720 shares had fallen to about 1,000 livres; notes were cut to 50% of face value
Law fled France in December 1720 (died poor in Venice in 1729)

caption:
Paris, 1719: Mississippi Company shares went from 500 to about 10,000 livres in roughly a year.
The twist: John Law's own bank printed the paper notes that paid for them. By December 1720 the share was near 1,000.
